rv.q: Matthew Warchus’s beautifully controlled and intelligent production is all shifting nuance and finely calibrated detail...
The joy of the evening lies in watching Fiennes at the height of his powers and relishing a play that offers one of the most searing self-portraits in drama.
The result is a production that edges towards the three-hour mark but speaks hauntingly about the dark heart of ambition and the madness of desire.
Fiennes, looking more and more like DH Lawrence, conveys knotty intensity, irascible solipsism and a man slipping away from himself.
The Master Builder at The Old Vic not only does justice to Ibsen but is theatre at its best: bold, relevant, brilliantly acted and compelling.
The two leads are extraordinary as is the direction.
It’s a magnificent, uncompromising performance, crackling with fire and rancid with guilt and nastiness.
Fiennes is terrific as Solness, anchoring himself to the floor in the face of the domestic storm raging around him.

The strongest moments of the play come at its most unhinged, when the language becomes untethered and Snook is possessed by an exhortive passion, spiralling hysterically well past the play’s climactic moment.

cn.t: Critics largely praise Ralph Fiennes' magnetic, commanding performance in this Ibsen revival, with Hare's adaptation also drawing acclaim. A minority find the play itself preposterous, making reception slightly mixed overall.
